listen_text: Section. Introduction. We have a semantics for the basic modal language in terms of modal models, and a notion of a formula being valid—true at all worlds in all models—or valid with respect to some class of models or frames—true at all worlds in all models in the class, or based on the frame. Logic usually connects such semantic characterizations of validity with a proof-theoretic notion of derivability. The aim is to define a notion of derivability in some system such that a formula is derivable if and only if it is valid. The simplest and historically oldest derivation systems are so-called Hilbert-type or axiomatic derivation systems. Hilbert-type derivation systems for many modal logics are relatively easy to construct: they are simple as objects of metatheoretical study (for example, to prove soundness and completeness). However, they are much harder to use to prove formulas in than, say, natural deduction systems. In Hilbert-type derivation systems, a derivation of a formula is a sequence of formulas leading from certain axioms, via a handful of inference rules, to the formula in question. Since we want the derivation system to match the semantics, we have to guarantee that the set of derivable formulas are true in all models (or true in all models in which all axioms are true). We'll first isolate some properties of modal logics that are necessary for this to work: the “normal” modal logics. For normal modal logics, there are only two inference rules that need to be assumed: modus ponens and necessitation. As axioms we take all (substitution instances) of tautologies, and, depending on the modal logic we deal with, a number of modal axioms. Even if we are just interested in the class of all models, we must also count all substitution instances of axiom K and axiom dual as axioms. This alone generates the minimal normal modal logic modal system K . Definition. The rule of modus ponens is the inference schema Source premise node one: formula A . listen_text: Section. Soundness. A derivation system is called sound if everything that can be derived is valid. When considering modal systems, that is, derivations where in addition to axiom K we can use instances of some formulas A subscript one , and so on, formula A subscript n , we want every derivable formula to be true in any model in which formula A subscript one , and so on, formula A subscript n are true. Theorem. Soundness Theorem. If every instance of formula A subscript one , and so on, formula A subscript n is valid in the classes of models class C of models subscript one , and so on, class C of models subscript n , respectively, then modal system K formula A subscript one and so on formula A subscript n derives formula B implies that formula B is valid in the class of models class C of models subscript one intersected with and so on intersected with class C of models subscript n . End theorem. Proof. By induction on length of proofs. For brevity, put class C of models equals class C of models subscript one intersected with and so on intersected with class C of models subscript n . List. Next item. Induction Basis: If formula B has a proof of length one , then it is either a tautological instance, an instance of axiom K, or of Dual, or an instance of one of formula A subscript one , and so on, formula A subscript n . In the first case, formula B is valid in class C of models , since tautological instance are valid in any class of models, by the proposition that tautological instances are valid . Similarly in the second case, by the proposition that axiom K is valid and the proposition that the duality schema is valid . Finally in the third case, since formula B is valid in class C of models subscript i and class C of models is a subset of class C of models subscript i , we have that formula B is valid in class C of models as well by the proposition preserving validity under subclasses of models . Next item. Inductive step: Suppose formula B has a proof of length k is greater than one . If formula B is a tautological instance or an instance of one of formula A subscript one , and so on, formula A subscript n , we proceed as in the previous step. So suppose formula B is obtained by modus ponens from previous formulas C implies formula B and formula C . Then formula C implies formula B and formula C have proofs of length is less than k , and by inductive hypothesis they are valid in class C of models . By the soundness of modus ponens , formula B is valid in class C of models as well. Finally suppose formula B is obtained by necessitation from formula C (so that formula B equals box formula C ). By inductive hypothesis, formula C is valid in class C of models , and by the validity-preservation rule for necessitation so is formula B . End list. End proof. End section.
